Chapter 6. The Myth of the “Good Victim” and the Limits of Sympathy.
You ever notice that quiet, unspoken rule in our justice system? It’s like—only a certain kind of victim really gets our sympathy. The law, and the folks who make it, draw these invisible lines between people they believe deserve compassion, and those they don’t. And if you’re on the wrong side of that line? You’re often left standing alone, unheard, and unprotected.
Imagine a mother whose son has been shot. She stands in front of a crowd, her grief so raw you can almost feel it. But instead of comfort, she’s bombarded with questions about her son—what kind of friends did he have, what choices did he make, what music did he listen to? The message is pretty clear: if he wasn’t perfect, maybe he somehow brought this on himself.
The legal system? It asks those same questions, digging for reasons to hold back empathy.
Most folks don’t even realize how this logic slips into every part of the system. When a Black person is harmed, the first reaction is often to look for flaws—to find some reason to question their innocence. This whole idea of the “good victim” becomes a shield for keeping things just as they are. It lets us avoid facing the deeper roots of violence and injustice.
Think about a young woman who’s been assaulted. She hesitates to call the police, already knowing her own record will be thrown back in her face. And when she finally does reach out, the officers seem more interested in her past than in what happened to her. Suddenly, the courtroom isn’t a place for healing—it’s a place where her pain gets weighed against her mistakes, where her worthiness is constantly under scrutiny.
You start to realize that the law’s sympathy only goes out to those who fit a narrow mold. The rest? They’re left to fend for themselves, their suffering brushed off as just the price of poor choices. But this isn’t just a lack of empathy—it’s a failure of justice.
It’s so easy to fall into the trap of thinking only the blameless deserve help. But here’s something to remember: everyone carries scars. Everyone’s made mistakes. If justice only shows up for perfection, then almost nobody gets real justice. The real challenge is creating a system that sees the full humanity in every person, no matter what’s in their past.
For those denied sympathy, that pain doesn’t just fade after the verdict. It sticks with them—a sharp reminder that, to the law, some lives seem to matter more than others.
So, the fight for justice? It’s really about expanding our circle of care. It’s about seeing the dignity in every single story.
Because until the law learns to offer compassion without conditions, the promise of equal justice is always going to feel a little bit empty.
